intro: Chronic low back pain motivates the development of personalized computational spine models. Musculoskeletal (MS) models estimate motion and muscle forces, whereas finite element (FE) models resolve local tissue stresses and strains. This research explores a person-specific integrated approach that combines the complementary strengths of both representations.
inputs: The workflow draws on person-specific anatomical imaging and model inputs to represent the lumbar spine within a whole-body biomechanical framework. Imaging supports individualized geometry rather than relying solely on a generic anatomical model.
development: The chapter develops a biologically assisted integrated model connecting a whole-body musculoskeletal representation to a detailed lumbar spine representation. The workflow includes preprocessing, model construction, and simulation using the computational tools described in the dissertation.
personal: MRI-derived lumbar anatomy is used to personalize vertebral and intervertebral disc geometry. The model represents major lumbar structures, including vertebrae, discs, ligaments, and facet joints, to investigate how spinal loads are distributed.
mesh: Flexion was the most mesh-sensitive evaluated task. The reported von Mises stress difference was 27.3% between Mesh I and Mesh III, but only 1.5% between Mesh III and Mesh IV. Mesh III was selected as a practical balance of solution time and numerical convergence; differences between Mesh III and IV remained below 5% throughout the model.
validation: The L4–L5 range of motion predicted using FE and MS disc representations was compared with published in-vitro measurements under 500 N compression and moments up to 10 Nm. Both representations generally followed the experimental ranges in flexion, lateral bending, and axial rotation. Both predicted a stiffer response in extension than the referenced experimental measurements.
stress: Under 500 N compression and a 10 Nm moment, the L4–L5 disc showed loading-direction-dependent stress patterns. Flexion and extension concentrated stress in anterior and posterior regions; lateral bending increased stress laterally; and axial rotation produced a more broadly distributed increase. Fiber stresses also varied with motion direction: posterior fibers were tensioned in flexion, anterior fibers in extension, and opposing sides responded differently in bending and rotation.
discussion: The integrated modeling approach is intended to connect personalized anatomy, whole-body dynamics, and detailed disc mechanics. The chapter identifies further validation during realistic movements, including bending, rotation, and lifting, as an important next step.
conclusion: The chapter presents a person-specific lumbar spine modeling workflow combining imaging-based anatomy with musculoskeletal and finite element approaches. It includes vertebrae, discs, ligaments, and facet joints, and investigates two representations of disc mechanics. The work establishes a foundation for estimating individualized spinal tissue loading and for further validation during dynamic activities.
